78-r1.sourceTitle: Complex Analysis (Howell & Mathews), Section 6.3 The Cauchy-Goursat Theorem
78-r1.locator: Section 6.3, Theorem 6.3.6, second proof (Goursat's proof), Eqs. (6.3.7)-(6.3.11)
78-r1.proofSketch: Prove the theorem first for a triangle C. Joining midpoints of the sides splits C into four positively oriented triangles whose interior edges cancel, so the integral over C is the sum of the four integrals, and one of them, C_1, has modulus at least a quarter of the total. Iterating gives nested triangles C_n with $|\int_C f| \le 4^n |\int_{C_n} f|$, shrinking to a point $z_0$ where f is differentiable. Writing $f(z)=f(z_0)+f'(z_0)(z-z_0)+\eta(z)(z-z_0)$ with $\eta\to 0$, the linear part integrates to zero over the closed triangle, so $\int_{C_n} f=\int_{C_n}\eta(z)(z-z_0)\,dz$. Since $L_n=2^{-n}L$ and $|z-z_0|<L_n/2$, the estimate gives $|\int_C f|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$, hence zero. Polygons follow by triangulating, and general simple closed contours by polygonal approximation (details omitted in the source).

Goursat's proof, second half: epsilon estimate, polygonal and general contours (Sec. 6.3)

78-r2.sourceTitle: Complex Analysis (Howell & Mathews), Section 6.3 The Cauchy-Goursat Theorem
78-r2.locator: Section 6.3, Theorem 6.3.6, first proof (Cauchy's proof), Eqs. (6.3.4)-(6.3.6)
78-r2.proofSketch: Assume additionally that $f'$ is continuous. Writing $f=u+iv$, the contour integral splits as $\int_C u\,dx - v\,dy + i\int_C v\,dx+u\,dy$. Green's theorem turns the real part into $\iint_R(-v_x-u_y)\,dx\,dy$ and the imaginary part into $\iint_R(u_x-v_y)\,dx\,dy$, where R is the interior of C. The Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ make both integrands zero, so $\int_C f\,dz=0$.
78-r2.attribution: Russell W. Howell and John H. Mathews, Complex Analysis for Mathematics and Engineering, Section 6.3, https://complexanalysis.org/web/sec_cauchy-goursat.html
78-r2.transcriptionNotes: Proof of Green's theorem (collapsed on the page) is not included; the source requires f' continuous for this proof.

78-r3.sourceTitle: Complex Analysis (Howell & Mathews), Section 6.4 The Fundamental Theorems of Integration
78-r3.locator: Section 6.4, Theorem 6.4.1 (existence of antiderivative on a simply connected domain), proof
78-r3.proofSketch: For f analytic on a simply connected domain D, fix $z_0$ and set $F(z)=\int_{z_0}^z f(\xi)\,d\xi$. Path independence: two contours $C_1,C_2$ from $z_0$ to $z$ give a closed contour $C_1-C_2$ whose integral vanishes by the Cauchy-Goursat theorem, so F is well defined. For the derivative, $F(z+\Delta z)-F(z)=\int_\Gamma f$ over the segment from z to $z+\Delta z$, and since $\int_\Gamma f(z)\,d\xi=f(z)\Delta z$, continuity of f gives $|(F(z+\Delta z)-F(z))/\Delta z - f(z)|<\varepsilon$. Hence $F'=f$.

images.caption: Theorem 6.4.1 and first half of proof: path independence from Cauchy-Goursat (Sec. 6.4)

78-r3.attribution: Russell W. Howell and John H. Mathews, Complex Analysis for Mathematics and Engineering, Section 6.4, https://complexanalysis.org/web/sec_integration-theorems.html
78-r3.transcriptionNotes: Source gives the primitive argument (path independence via Cauchy-Goursat, then F'=f) but does not use homotopy invariance; simply connected is defined by 'no holes'. Figures 6.4.2 and 6.4.3 not captured.
